claim: VRC01-class bNAb family derived from the VH1-2*02 germline allele arose in multiple HIV-1–infected donors.
source: The VRC01-class bNAb family derived from the VH1-2*02 germline allele arose in multiple HIV-1–infected donors, yet targets the CD4-binding site on Env with common interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies that identified these antibodies in multiple donors.

claim: VRC01-class bNAbs target the CD4-binding site on Env with common interactions.
source: The VRC01-class bNAb family derived from the VH1-2*02 germline allele arose in multiple HIV-1–infected donors, yet targets the CD4-binding site on Env with common interactions.
evidence: This is supported by structural and functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Modified forms of the 426c Env activate germline-reverted B cell receptors.
source: Modified forms of the 426c Env that activate germline-reverted B cell receptors are candidate immunogens for eliciting VRC01-class bNAbs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing binding of germline antibodies to 426c immunogens.

claim: Germline bNAb–426c gp120 complexes showed preservation of VRC01-class signature residues and gp120 contacts.
source: Germline bNAb–426c gp120 complexes showed preservation of VRC01-class signature residues and gp120 contacts, but detectably different binding modes compared to mature bNAb-gp120 complexes.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from crystal structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Germline bNAb–426c gp120 complexes showed detectably different binding modes compared to mature bNAb-gp120 complexes.
source: Germline bNAb–426c gp120 complexes showed preservation of VRC01-class signature residues and gp120 contacts, but detectably different binding modes compared to mature bNAb-gp120 complexes.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons and angle of approach analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: VRC01-class germline antibodies exhibited preformed antigen-binding conformations for recognizing immunogens.
source: Unlike typical antibody-antigen interactions, VRC01–class germline antibodies exhibited preformed antigen-binding conformations for recognizing immunogens.
evidence: This is supported by structural superimpositions showing minimal conformational changes between bound and unbound germline antibodies.

claim: Affinity maturation introduced substitutions increasing induced-fit recognition.
source: Affinity maturation introduced substitutions increasing induced-fit recognition and electropositivity, potentially to accommodate negatively-charged complex-type N-glycans on gp120.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons between germline and mature antibodies showing increased conformational flexibility in mature forms.

claim: Affinity maturation introduced substitutions increasing electropositivity, potentially to accommodate negatively-charged complex-type N-glycans on gp120.
source: Affinity maturation introduced substitutions increasing induced-fit recognition and electropositivity, potentially to accommodate negatively-charged complex-type N-glycans on gp120.
evidence: This is supported by electrostatic potential calculations showing increased positive charge in mature antibodies.

claim: The HIV-1 envelope spike is a trimer of gp120-gp41 heterodimers.
source: The HIV-1 envelope (Env) spike, a trimer of gp120-gp41 heterodimers, is the only target of neutralizing antibodies (Abs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of HIV-1 virology.

claim: The HIV-1 envelope spike is the only target of neutralizing antibodies.
source: The HIV-1 envelope (Env) spike, a trimer of gp120-gp41 heterodimers, is the only target of neutralizing antibodies (Abs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of HIV-1 virology.

claim: Rapid mutation combined with structural features of the Env trimer result in induction of mainly strain-specific neutralizing Abs in most infected individuals.
source: Rapid mutation combined with structural features of the Env trimer that hide conserved features of the HIV-1 spike result in induction of mainly strain-specific neutralizing Abs in most infected individuals.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Broadly neutralizing Abs evolve in a minority of HIV-1–infected individuals after several years of infection.
source: However, broadly neutralizing Abs (bNAbs) evolve in a minority of HIV-1–infected individuals after several years of infection.
evidence: This is supported by epidemiological studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Highly potent bNAbs against the conserved CD4-binding site on gp120 derived from the VH1-2*02 variable heavy chain gene have been isolated from at least nine HIV-1–infected individuals.
source: Highly potent bNAbs against the conserved CD4-binding site (CD4bs) on gp120 that were derived from the VH1-2*02 variable heavy chain (HC) gene have been isolated from at least nine HIV-1–infected individuals (Scheid et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; 2015; Wu et al., 2011; Georgiev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies that isolated these antibodies.

claim: VRC01-class bNAbs exhibit unusually high levels of somatic hypermutation, with changes in both complementarity determining regions and framework regions.
source: These bNAbs exhibit unusually high levels of somatic hypermutation, with changes in both complementarity determining regions (CDRs) and framework regions (FWRs) (Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study analyzing somatic hypermutation in these antibodies.

claim: VRC01-class bNAbs share a common mode of gp120 binding in which the VH1-2*02-derived variable heavy domain mimics CD4.
source: As exemplified by VRC01, the first such bNAb to be isolated (Wu et al., 2010), VRC01-class bNAbs share a common mode of gp120 binding in which the VH1-2*02-derived variable heavy (VH) domain mimics CD4 (Wu et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2010; 2013; 2015; Diskin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Signature features of the HCs of VRC01-class bNAbs include Trp50HC, Asn58HC, and Arg71HC.
source: Signature features of the HCs of VRC01-class bNAbs that explain their derivation from the VH1-02*02 gene segment include Trp50HC, Asn58HC, and Arg71HC; an additional signature residue, Trp100BHC within CDRH3, is derived from the joining of the D and J gene segments to the VH gene segment during V(D)J recombination (Diskin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing these signature residues.

claim: Trp100BHC within CDRH3 is derived from the joining of the D and J gene segments to the VH gene segment during V(D)J recombination.
source: Signature features of the HCs of VRC01-class bNAbs that explain their derivation from the VH1-02*02 gene segment include Trp50HC, Asn58HC, and Arg71HC; an additional signature residue, Trp100BHC within CDRH3, is derived from the joining of the D and J gene segments to the VH gene segment during V(D)J recombination (Diskin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing these signature residues.

claim: The variable light domains of VRC01-class bNAbs require a short (five residues) CDRL3 loop to allow interactions with gp120 V5 and loop D.
source: The variable light (VL) domains of VRC01-class bNAbs, which can be derived from several different VL germline gene segments, require a short (five residues) CDRL3 loop to allow interactions with gp120 V5 and loop D (Diskin et al., 2012) and often include a deletion in CDRL1 to avoid clashes with an N-linked glycan attached to Asn276gp120 (Zhou et al., 2010; 2013; Scharf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: VRC01-class bNAbs often include a deletion in CDRL1 to avoid clashes with an N-linked glycan attached to Asn276gp120.
source: The variable light (VL) domains of VRC01-class bNAbs, which can be derived from several different VL germline gene segments, require a short (five residues) CDRL3 loop to allow interactions with gp120 V5 and loop D (Diskin et al., 2012) and often include a deletion in CDRL1 to avoid clashes with an N-linked glycan attached to Asn276gp120 (Zhou et al., 2010; 2013; Scharf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The LC contact residues of VRC01-like bNAbs and the short CDRL3 are not germline encoded.
source: The LC contact residues of VRC01-like bNAbs and the short CDRL3 are not germline encoded (Diskin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study analyzing germline sequences.

claim: The first step in eliciting an Ab is binding to its precursor germline-encoded B cell receptor by an antigen or immunogen with adequate affinity to initiate B cell activation and affinity maturation.
source: The first step in eliciting an Ab is binding to its precursor germline-encoded B cell receptor by an antigen or immunogen with adequate affinity to initiate B cell activation and affinity maturation (Batista and Neuberger, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on B cell activation.

claim: Germline-reverted versions of VRC01-class bNAbs do not bind to Env trimers or to gp120.
source: Although the unmutated VH1-2*02 gene segment includes the signature VH domain residues for interacting with the CD4bs, germline-reverted versions of VRC01-class bNAbs do not bind to Env trimers or to gp120 (Scheid et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2010; Diskin et al., 2012; Scharf et al., 2013; Hoot et al., 2013; Ota et al., 2012; McGuire et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to binding studies.

claim: NIH45-46GL contained 40 HC and 23 LC substitutions in addition to a two-residue insertion in CDRL1 compared with mature NIH45-46.
source: Compared with mature NIH45-46 (NIH45-46MAT), NIH45-46GL contained 40 HC and 23 LC substitutions in addition to a two-residue insertion in CDRL1.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 3BNC60GL contained 38 HC and 25 LC substitutions in addition to a four-residue deletion in HC framework region 3 and a four-residue insertion in CDRL1 compared with 3BNC60MAT.
source: 3BNC60GL contained 38 HC and 25 LC substitutions in addition to a four-residue deletion in HC framework region 3 (FWR3HC) and a four-residue insertion in CDRL1 compared with 3BNC60MAT (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1.

claim: 426c.TM1△V1-3 binds to germline VRC01 and NIH45-46.
source: 426c.TM1△V1-3 binds to germline VRC01 and NIH45-46 (McGuire et al., 2013; 2014), and 426c.TM4△V1-3 binds to germline versions of 12A21, 3BNC60, VRC-CH31, VRC-PG19 and VRC-PG20 in addition to germline VRC01 and NIH45-46 (McGuire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to binding studies.

claim: 426c.TM4△V1-3 binds to germline versions of 12A21, 3BNC60, VRC-CH31, VRC-PG19 and VRC-PG20 in addition to germline VRC01 and NIH45-46.
source: 426c.TM1△V1-3 binds to germline VRC01 and NIH45-46 (McGuire et al., 2013; 2014), and 426c.TM4△V1-3 binds to germline versions of 12A21, 3BNC60, VRC-CH31, VRC-PG19 and VRC-PG20 in addition to germline VRC01 and NIH45-46 (McGuire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to binding studies.

claim: Germline-reverted Abs did not bind detectably to 93TH057 gp120.
source: As expected, the germline-reverted Abs did not bind detectably to 93TH057 gp120, but NIH45-46GL bound to both 426c.TM1ΔV1-3 and 426c.TM4ΔV1-3 gp120s with equilibrium dissociation constants (KDs) of ~0.7 and 3 μM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data presented in Figure 2.

claim: NIH45-46GL bound to both 426c.TM1ΔV1-3 and 426c.TM4ΔV1-3 gp120s with equilibrium dissociation constants of ~0.7 and 3 μM, respectively.
source: As expected, the germline-reverted Abs did not bind detectably to 93TH057 gp120, but NIH45-46GL bound to both 426c.TM1ΔV1-3 and 426c.TM4ΔV1-3 gp120s with equilibrium dissociation constants (KDs) of ~0.7 and 3 μM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data presented in Figure 2.

claim: 3BNC60GL did not bind to 426c.TM1ΔV1-3.
source: As previously described (McGuire et al., 2013; 2014), 3BNC60GL did not bind to 426c.TM1ΔV1-3, but showed detectable binding to 426c.TM4ΔV1-3 gp120.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data presented in Figure 2 and citations to previous studies.

claim: 3BNC60GL showed detectable binding to 426c.TM4ΔV1-3 gp120.
source: As previously described (McGuire et al., 2013; 2014), 3BNC60GL did not bind to 426c.TM1ΔV1-3, but showed detectable binding to 426c.TM4ΔV1-3 gp120.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data presented in Figure 2.

claim: NIH45-46MAT and 3BNC60MAT bound to all gp120s with nM or higher affinity.
source: By contrast, NIH45-46MAT and 3BNC60MAT bound to all gp120s with nM or higher affinity (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Crystal structures of NIH45-46GL bound to 426c.TM1△V1-3 and 3BNC60GL bound to 426c.TM4△V1-3 were solved to 3.4 Å and 3.1 Å resolution, respectively.
source: Crystal structures of NIH45-46GL bound to 426c.TM1△V1-3 and 3BNC60GL bound to 426c.TM4△V1-3 were solved to 3.4 Å and 3.1 Å resolution, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: Structures of unbound 3BNC60GL and 426c.TM4△V1-3 were solved at 1.9 Å and 2.0 Å resolution, respectively.
source: We also solved structures of unbound 3BNC60GL and 426c.TM4△V1-3 (at 1.9 Å and 2.0 Å resolution, respectively), and a complex structure of a 426c.TM4△V1-3 bound to 3BNC55MAT, a mature VRC01-class Ab (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: Superimpositions of bound and unbound forms of NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL Fabs and bound and unbound VRC01GL revealed no major structural changes.
source: Superimpositions of bound and unbound forms of NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL Fabs (this study) and bound and unbound VRC01GL (Jardine et al., 2013) revealed no major structural changes (Figure 3A,C,E).
evidence: This is supported by structural superimposition data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Root mean square deviations for superimposing all Cα atoms in the VHVL domains of bound and unbound Fabs of NIH45-46GL, 3BNC60GL, and VRC01GL were low (0.54 Å–0.73 Å).
source: Root mean square deviations (rmsds) for superimposing all Cα atoms in the VHVL domains of bound and unbound Fabs of NIH45-46GL, 3BNC60GL, and VRC01GL were low (0.54 Å–0.73 Å) (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis data presented in Figure 3K.

claim: The association of the VH and VL domains and the conformations of the CDR loops and surrounding FWRs found in the unbound forms were largely maintained in the germline-inferred Abs upon binding to their antigens.
source: Thus the association of the VH and VL domains and the conformations of the CDR loops and surrounding FWRs found in the unbound forms were largely maintained in the germline-inferred Abs upon binding to their antigens.
evidence: This is inferred from the low RMSD values and structural comparisons.

claim: Mature bNAbs exhibited more antigen binding-induced conformational flexibility within individual CDR loops and/or the FWRs than the germline-inferred Abs.
source: Thus the mature bNAbs (NIH45-46MAT, 3BNC60MAT, and VRC01MAT) are overall largely preformed to recognize antigen, but exhibited more antigen binding-induced conformational flexibility within individual CDR loops and/or the FWRs than the germline-inferred Abs.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons showing conformational changes in mature antibodies.

claim: No major structural rearrangements resulted from binding of either a germline or mature Ab to 426c.TM4△V1-3.
source: We found no major structural rearrangements resulting from binding of either a germline or mature Ab (Figure 3J,K), suggesting that the 426c gp120 core immunogens are preformed for binding to germline and mature forms of VRC01-class Abs.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The 426c gp120 core immunogens are preformed for binding to germline and mature forms of VRC01-class Abs.
source: We found no major structural rearrangements resulting from binding of either a germline or mature Ab (Figure 3J,K), suggesting that the 426c gp120 core immunogens are preformed for binding to germline and mature forms of VRC01-class Abs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of structural rearrangements upon binding.

claim: Both NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL interacted with the CD4-binding loop on gp120 using conserved interactions that mimic CD4 binding.
source: In particular, both NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL interacted with the CD4-binding loop on gp120 using conserved interactions that mimic CD4 binding, first described for the complex of VRC01MAT with 93TH057 gp120 (Zhou et al., 2010), in which VRC01-class bNAbs mimic CD4 using backbone atoms in the VH domain C" strand to engage with the CD4-binding loop on gp120 (Wu et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2010; 2015; Diskin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL make all predicted HC VRC01-class signature contacts with the CD4-binding loop, the V5 loop, and loop D to bind to gp120.
source: In summary, NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL make all predicted HC VRC01-class signature contacts with the CD4-binding loop, the V5 loop, and loop D to bind to gp120.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the antibody-gp120 interfaces.

claim: Comparison of the NIH45-46GL/426c.TM1△V1-3 and 3BNC60GL/426c.TM4△V1-3 structures with their mature counterparts revealed no major structural differences between the LC contacts with gp120 cores.
source: Comparison of the NIH45-46GL/426c.TM1△V1-3 and 3BNC60GL/426c.TM4△V1-3 structures with their mature counterparts (NIH45-46MAT/93TH057 and 3BNC117MAT/93TH057; PDB codes 3U7Y and 4JPV) revealed no major structural differences between the LC contacts with gp120 cores (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The greater number of residues in the CDRL1s in the germline Fab-containing complexes result in wider, rather than longer, loops than their mature counterparts.
source: The greater number of residues in the CDRL1s in the germline Fab-containing complexes (two and four additional residues in NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL, respectively) result in wider, rather than longer, loops than their mature counterparts (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: The superimposed germline Fabs showed no clashes between CDRL1 and ordered Asn276gp120 glycan residues.
source: The superimposed germline Fabs showed no clashes between CDRL1 and ordered Asn276gp120 glycan residues (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by structural superimposition analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: The surface area buried on gp120 by both germline Fabs was only slightly smaller than that buried by the corresponding mature Abs.
source: The surface area buried on gp120 by both germline Fabs was only slightly smaller than that buried by the corresponding mature Abs (1,039 Å2 vs. 1,190 Å2 for NIH45-46GL vs. NIH45-46MAT and 939 Å2 vs. 1,033 Å2 for 3BNC60GL vs. 3BNC117MAT), with gains in buried surface area in loop D, inner domain and bridging sheet residues of gp120 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by buried surface area calculations presented in Figure 6.

claim: The germline Fab complexes with the 426c gp120 immunogens exhibited larger rotations and translations relative to the VRC01 reference structure.
source: The germline Fab complexes with the 426c gp120 immunogens exhibited larger rotations and translations relative to the VRC01 reference structure, with the VRC01GL/eOD-GT6 complex showing an intermediate orientation.
evidence: This is supported by angle of approach analysis presented in Figure 7.

claim: The different orientation of the 3BNC60GL VH domain with respect to gp120 moves it away from the adjacent gp120 subunit, suggesting this orientation would be sterically compatible when binding to Env trimer.
source: This alignment suggests that the different orientation of the 3BNC60GL VH domain with respect to gp120 moves it away from the adjacent gp120 subunit, suggesting this orientation would be sterically compatible when binding to Env trimer.
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling of the antibody-trimer interaction.

claim: Comparisons of electrostatic surface potentials revealed a striking shift to more positively-charged antigen combining sites due to maturation.
source: Comparisons of electrostatic surface potentials revealed a striking shift to more positively-charged antigen combining sites due to maturation (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by electrostatic potential calculations presented in Figure 8.

claim: The more negatively-charged or neutral properties of the antigen-binding sites of the germline Fabs may interfere with interactions with complex-type N-glycans on gp120 containing negatively-charged sialic acids.
source: The more negatively-charged (3BNC60GL) or neutral (NIH45-46GL, VRC01GL) properties of the antigen-binding sites of the germline Fabs may interfere with interactions with complex-type N-glycans on gp120 containing negatively-charged sialic acids; in particular, the Asn276gp120 carbohydrate, typically a complex-type N-glycan (Binley et al., 2010; Go et al., 2011), would likely make unfavorable interactions with the neutral or negatively charged surfaces of 3BNC60GL, NIH45-46GL, or VRC01GL Fabs.
evidence: This is inferred from electrostatic potential analysis and knowledge of glycan properties.

claim: Mature VRC01-class bNAbs appear on average to have a higher net nominal charge of their VHVL domains (+4.9) than the average human Ab (+3.1).
source: Mature VRC01-class bNAbs appear on average to have a higher net nominal charge of their VHVL domains (+4.9) than the average human Ab (+3.1; as calculated from sequenced human B-cell repertoires) (Table 2) (Rubelt et al., 2012), and the VH1-2*02 gene segment yields a sequence with a nominal net charge of +5, higher than the average human VH gene segment (+2 to +3).
evidence: This is supported by charge calculations presented in Table 2 and citation to B-cell repertoire data.

claim: The VH1-2*02 gene segment yields a sequence with a nominal net charge of +5, higher than the average human VH gene segment (+2 to +3).
source: Mature VRC01-class bNAbs appear on average to have a higher net nominal charge of their VHVL domains (+4.9) than the average human Ab (+3.1; as calculated from sequenced human B-cell repertoires) (Table 2) (Rubelt et al., 2012), and the VH1-2*02 gene segment yields a sequence with a nominal net charge of +5, higher than the average human VH gene segment (+2 to +3).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison to human repertoire data.

claim: Evolution of increased electropositivity during maturation of VRC01-class bNAbs facilitates interactions with heavily glycosylated HIV-1 Env spikes that include complex N-linked glycans containing negatively charged sialic acids.
source: We suggest that evolution of increased electropositivity during maturation of VRC01-class bNAbs (and perhaps other HIV-1 bNAbs; Figure 8—figure supplement 1) facilitates interactions with heavily glycosylated HIV-1 Env spikes that include complex N-linked glycans containing negatively charged sialic acids.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on electrostatic analysis and knowledge of glycan properties.

claim: The neutral or negatively charged character of the germline Fab combining sites provides a structural justification for the necessity to eliminate the Asn276gp120- and Asn463gp120-linked N-glycans from eOD- and gp120-based immunogen candidates to achieve binding to inferred germline B-cell receptors.
source: In addition to these steric considerations for potentially unfavorable interactions between CDRL1 and the Asn276gp120-linked glycan, the neutral or negatively charged character of the germline Fab combining sites provides a structural justification for the necessity to eliminate the Asn276gp120- and Asn463gp120-linked N-glycans from eOD- and gp120-based immunogen candidates to achieve binding to inferred germline B-cell receptors (McGuire et al., 2013; Jardine et al., 2013; 2015; McGuire et al., 2014; 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from electrostatic analysis and supported by citations to immunogen design studies.

claim: A natural VRC01-class eliciting antigen could involve viral variants that lack the Asn276gp120 and the Asn463gp120 N-glycans.
source: The structures presented here, taken together with immunogen requirements for achieving germline Ab binding and previous structural analyses of mature VRC01-class Abs (Zhou et al., undefined; Zhou et al., 2010; 2013; McGuire et al., 2013; 2014; 2016; Jardine et al., 2013; 2015), suggest that the initiating antigen(s) in a natural pathway to induce VRC01-class Abs in HIV-1–infected individuals involve viral variants that lack the Asn276gp120 (5% of HIV-1 strains in the Los Alamos Database) and the Asn463gp120N-glycans (~80% of HIV-1 strains in the Los Alamos Database) (http://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/index).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and database information.

claim: A natural VRC01-class eliciting antigen could be the result of glycan heterogeneity within a single HIV-1 strain that produced variants containing high mannose, rather than complex-type, N-glycans at Asn276gp120 and/or Asn463gp120.
source: Alternatively, a natural VRC01-class eliciting antigen could be the result of glycan heterogeneity within a single HIV-1 strain that produced variants containing high mannose, rather than complex-type, N-glycans at Asn276gp120 and/or Asn463gp120, consistent with observations of glycan heterogeneity at individual N-linked glycosylation sites within single HIV-1 strains (Go et al., 2011; Behrens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and supported by citations to glycan heterogeneity studies.

claim: Germline precursors to affinity-matured Abs have been suggested to display structural flexibility to allow expanded antigen recognition through induced fit mechanisms.
source: Although antibody-antigen recognition modes represent a continuum of binding mechanisms, germline precursors to affinity-matured Abs have been suggested to display structural flexibility to allow expanded antigen recognition through induced fit mechanisms, whereas affinity maturation through somatic hypermutation was assumed to convert recognition to a lock-and-key model (Foote and Milstein, 1994; Wedemayer et al., 1997; Thorpe and Brooks, 2007).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies on antibody-antigen recognition.

claim: The maturation pathway for antigen binding from germline Ab to affinity-matured Ab does not involve changes from induced fit to lock-and-key binding mechanisms for VRC01 class of CD4bs bNAbs.
source: Here, we showed that for the VRC01 class of CD4bs bNAbs, the maturation pathway for antigen binding from germline Ab to affinity-matured Ab does not involve changes from induced fit to lock-and-key binding mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis showing preformed binding conformations in germline antibodies.

claim: The 426c gp120 immunogens bind NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL without requiring notable conformational changes in either the Ab or the antigen.
source: Instead, the 426c gp120 immunogens bind NIH45-46GL and 3BNC60GL without requiring notable conformational changes in either the Ab or the antigen; thus both are largely preformed for binding.
evidence: This is supported by structural superimposition data showing minimal conformational changes.

claim: The largely lock-and-key binding mechanism for germline VRC01-class recognition of antigen may be rationalized by the fact that germline VRC01-class CD4bs Abs face major steric constraints when binding to HIV-1 Env trimer.
source: The largely lock-and-key binding mechanism for germline VRC01-class recognition of antigen may be rationalized by the fact that germline VRC01-class CD4bs Abs face major steric constraints when binding to HIV-1 Env trimer due to the recessed location of the epitope and its shielding by glycans from the target and adjacent gp160 monomers (West et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and knowledge of Env trimer structure.

claim: The finding of lock-and-key recognition for germline Fabs binding to the 426c gp120 immunogens contrasts with recognition of unmodified gp120s used for structural studies of complexes with mature VRC01-class bNAbs.
source: The finding of what can be described as lock-and-key recognition for germline Fabs binding to the 426c gp120 immunogens contrasts with recognition of unmodified gp120s used for structural studies of complexes with mature VRC01-class bNAbs that do not bind or bind only poorly to germline Abs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural data from different antibody-gp120 complexes.

claim: The findings of lock-and-key style germline Fab recognition with increased flexibility upon maturation for the highly somatically-mutated VRC01-class bNAbs contradict the assumption of induced fit for germline Ab recognition and lock-and-key fit for mature Ab binding.
source: Taken together, the findings of what appears to be lock-and-key style germline Fab recognition with increased flexibility upon maturation for the highly somatically-mutated VRC01-class bNAbs contradict the assumption of induced fit for germline Ab recognition and lock-and-key fit for mature Ab binding (Foote and Milstein, 1994; Wedemayer et al., 1997; Thorpe and Brooks, 2007).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison to previous models of antibody maturation.

claim: 426c-based immunogens are able to bind germline precursors of VRC01-class bNAbs as a complete gp120 core because they can engage the unbound conformation of these Abs.
source: We speculate that 426c-based immunogens are able to bind germline precursors of VRC01-class bNAbs as a complete gp120 core because they can engage the unbound conformation of these Abs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis showing preformed binding conformations.

claim: The improved binding of the 426c-based gp120 immunogens to some germline VRC01-class Abs upon removal of the V1V2 and V3 loops could result from the removal of steric occlusion by the variable loops, removal of glycans attached to these loops, or a combination of these factors.
source: The improved binding of the 426c-based gp120 immunogens to some germline VRC01-class Abs upon removal of the V1V2 and V3 loops from the 426c.TM1△V1-3 and 426c.TM4△V1-3 gp120s could result from the removal of steric occlusion by the variable loops (also not present in the eOD immunogens (Jardine et al., 2013; 2015), and which may be flexible in the context of a gp120 or eOD), removal of glycans attached to these loops, or a combination of these factors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and binding data.

claim: A germline-binding antigen should be designed to be electrostatically compatible with the neutral or negatively charged antigen-binding surfaces of germline VRC01 Fabs.
source: Thus, our results suggest implementation of a general strategy in which a germline-binding antigen is designed to be electrostatically compatible with the neutral or negatively charged antigen-binding surfaces of germline VRC01 Fabs and to fit in lock-and-key mode to the combining site of a germline Fab, with consideration paid to the slightly different angles of approach reported here for germline Fab binding to the gp120-based immunogens.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the structural and electrostatic analysis presented.
